grant.title: Strategies and Technologies for Warning, Detection, and Prevention of Trespassing in the Vicinity of Highway-Rail Grade Crossings: State of the Practice and Research Needs
grant.abstract: The U.S. rail network is the largest, safest, and most efficient rail network in the world that operates over 160,000 rail miles. It plays a pivotal role in enabling the transportation of goods and people throughout the nation; and due to this crucial function, it serves as a fundamental pillar in supporting the economic expansion of the United States (Federal Railroad Administration, 2023). Simultaneously, the U.S. highway network plays a crucial role in enabling the seamless transportation of both individuals and cargo, consisting of a sophisticated linked grid of roads that spans the entire nation. According to data from the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT), the average monthly traffic volume for the year 2022 exceeded 3,000 billion miles. However, at the intersection of these two crucial transportation modes lies a point of concern—the Highway Rail Grade Crossing (HRGC). HRGCs are where a road or pathway intersects with a railway track. These crossings facilitate the safe passage of vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians across railway lines. However, if road users fail to notice warning signals and attempt to cross the tracks when a train is approaching, a catastrophic collision can occur, leading to severe injuries or fatalities. As such, HRGCs are a critical cause of hazardous conditions that may involve collisions between trains and vehicles or pedestrians. Thousands of highway-rail incidents occur in the US every year. Such incidents include many fatal crashes. Between 2010 and 2018, a total of 1,114 fatal crashes tragically occurred at HRGCs in the United States that resulted in the loss of 1,306 lives. Trespassing at-or-near HRGC is a major safety issue. Trespassers are most often pedestrians trying to take a shortcut and/or do not notice incoming trains. Although it is illegal, more than 400 rail trespass fatalities occur every year. Various technologies and practices have been proposed to detect trespassing at rail crossings. Such technologies can involve various types of sensors such as radar, laser, infrared, magnetic, and many others. Such technologies can be infrastructure-based, locomotive-based, or a combination of both. Some innovative technologies include CCTV cameras assisted by computer vision, depth-sensing cameras, stereo vision, laser systems, and smart sensors enabled by deep learning, among others. Naturally, various technologies and practices come with diverse considerations, including aspects like their reliability, cost-effectiveness, accuracy, and smooth integration into rail infrastructure systems. There is a need to explore the advantages and disadvantages of existing and emerging technologies considering the needs and challenges of the rail infrastructure. The outcomes of this exploratory investigation guide decision-making and future research to prevent trespassing at HRGCs and improve the safety of the U.S. rail network.

grant.abstract: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is located in the historic Texan borderlands created at the end of the Mexican-American war in 1848 which separated families on both sides of the Rio Grande River. The university was formed in 2013 when The University of Texas at Brownsville and The University of Texas Pan-American were consolidated to expand educational opportunities in the underserved and rural Valley of the Rio Grande. UTRGV is a major Hispanic-Serving Institution (HSI), primarily a nonresidential, 4-year, public, R2 institution, with campuses situated along the lower 100 miles of the Rio Grande. UTRGV's student demographics mirror those of the Lower Rio Grande Valley (RGV), with over 95% of our 32,000 students being of Hispanic or Latinx origin (Region One Education Service Center, 2021), and over 85% having Mexican-American heritage. Academic programs in engineering, started in 1992, were first accredited by ABET in 1996. The College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) currently has 6 departments offering 8 bachelors' and 7 masters' degrees. The college has over 110 faculty members and serves nearly 3900 students, mostly (90%) undergraduates. Although CECS does not have a PhD program yet, a pathway for a doctoral degree is offered jointly with the University of Nebraska at Lincoln (UNL). As the second largest HSI in the nation, UTR V is uniquely positioned to broaden the participation of Hispanics in the engineering workforce.

grant.abstract: - Preproposal submitted - The proposed project is to develop electrically conductive concrete pipes to remove soluble cationic contaminants from run-off water via electrochemical precipitation and to protect Texas water resources including the ocean water. Concrete pipes can become conductive with added graphite and precipitate soluble cations by binding with carbonate or hydroxide at the elevated pH around the cathodic conductive concrete pipes. Metallic anodes will be used in combination. The research team will look at the removal of water hardness and heavy metals (e.g., lead, chromium-6) by the proposed novel technology. Previous research at the PI’s lab has shown that the concrete block with graphite additives as a cathode can remove 20-30% of water hardness with titanium as an anode (Billah and Kim, 2020). This study needs to be expanded to gauge the applicability to treat contaminated run-off water thus protecting Texas natural water resources including the Gulf of Mexico. The specific objectives of the project are to: 1) Determine the optimum operational conditions (voltage, ampere, graphite contents, the distance between electrodes, etc.) of the electrically conductive concrete for the most efficient hardness removal. 2) Check if the electrically conductive concrete pipes can be used to remove hardness from the tap water under both batch and continuous flow conditions. Also, focuses will be given to changes in the concentration of chlorine disinfectant and acidity of tap water. 3) Check if other soluble heavy metals in the tap water can be removed from the electrically conductive concrete pipe operated under optimum conditions that will be determined from Task 1. 4) Provide the preliminary version of construction, installation, and operational/maintenance guidance.

grant.title: CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS)
grant.abstract: Overview: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) proposes to establish the “CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS).” The Center’s mission is to advance and transform the much-needed research and education at the nexus of automation, sensors, and artificial intelligence (AI), as integral parts of the “NSF’s 10 Big Ideas,” anticipating the revolutionary cyber-physical infrastructure systems (CIS). Three Colleges of Engineering, Sciences, and Education at UTRGV in collaboration with the Universities of Illinois (at Urbana-Champaign and at Chicago) and California (Riverside) will pursue multidisciplinary research on CIS, aiming to: (i) transfer technology to various transportation, logistics, manufacturing, and construction industries; and (ii) prepare a minority STEM workforce to drive future CIS-based communities. The Center envisions a portfolio of three research subprojects on automation, sensors, and AI that bridges diverse STEM disciplines. A holistic, multi-level approach is adopted to address CIS planning, design, and operation. While each subproject constitutes a unique element, their synergy ensures the CIS integrity. Subproject 1 pushes the frontiers of knowledge in future transportation infrastructure, which will be transformed by autonomous vehicles (AVs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), in six directions: (i) at the planning level, public acceptance and policy issues of (U)AV; (ii-iv) at the design level, computer vision, automatic navigation, and model/field-based testing of the designed capabilities; and (v, vi) at the operation level, human-(U)AV interactions and network-wide inter-(U)AV interactions. Subproject 2 designs and embeds sensors in CIS for two purposes. First, (U)AV sensors help perform automated tasks. Second, sensors in civil infrastructure and (U)AVs monitor infrastructure health. Three research areas are defined: (i, ii) at the design level, computational simulation, synthesis, and 3D printing of sensor materials and UAV structures, and (iii) at the operation level, cost-effective decision-making to upkeep infrastructure health using sensor data. Since (U)AVs and sensors will inherently generate big data, Subproject 3 will synchronously work with subprojects 1 and 2 to: (i) develop AI solutions for big data management, and (ii) develop AI algorithms for big data analytics and decision making in the design and operation of (U)AVs and infrastructure. UTRGV is the nation’s second largest Hispanic-Serving Institute (HIS) located in South Texas with an established record of preparing underrepresented minority students for STEM careers. The Center will provide (under)graduate students with cutting-edge CIS research experience, will integrate CIS research and education, and will pave a pathway from High School through graduate programs in STEM disciplines. This broad initiative at UTRGV will also offer new courses related to the subprojects. The Center will further enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV and will strengthen the research competitiveness of a diverse group of faculty. Intellectual Merit: The proposed self-sustaining Center will play a key role in transforming the scientific discoveries at the intersection of automation, sensors, and AI technologies, which are the integral elements of next-generation CIS. The Center will address current gaps in the planning, design, and operation of CIS by proposing innovative theoretical, computational, experimental, and empirical solutions spanning from micro (molecule)- to macro (system)-scale, which also yield practical solutions valuable for the industry. Broader Impacts: The Center’s research and education activities will develop an underrepresented workforce equipped with the skills to address complex societal problems. The Center will partner with the public and private sectors to advance technology transfer and product development in CIS. The Center’s activities are key for the establishment of an inaugural engineering doctoral program, which will be vital in elevating UTRGV to a Research I institution and advancing the CIS research agenda in a predominantly HSI. The Center's research findings will be made available to the research community as journal publications and conference proceedings, which will inform other domains undergoing related transformations, such as the health industry, manufacturing and production systems, and the military.

grant.title: Electrochemical precipitation of tap water from Lower Rio Grande Valley area with conductive concrete pipes.
grant.sponsor: EPA Annual P3 Awards: A National Student Design Competition Focusing on People, Prosperity and the Planet
grant.abstract: Objective: Tap water in LRGV is extremely hard with more than 350 mg/L as CaCO 3 . Also, there have been reports about heavy metals in drinking water in rural communities in Lower Rio Grande Valley (LRGV) area. Thus, residents in the region depended on bottled water and watermill for drinking water, which has imposed an economical burden on them. More so is witnessed from the economically depressed area like Colonias. The proposed project is designed to remove soluble cations like water hardness and heavy metals from the tap water to ensure economical, safe, and sustainable water resources to all the local municipalities in the LRGV area. The project team proposes to develop a novel in-situ electrochemical precipitation (EP) using conductive concrete pipes as a cathode and a metallic anode. If combined with solar power, the proposed technology will be an eco-friendly water softening and cleaning system with minimum maintenance. Description: The proposed P3 project will focus on developing a novel in-situ EP technology to remove soluble metallic contaminants from drinking water. It involves using conductive concrete as a cathode and a metallic anode in a batch or continuous flow condition. The research team in this proposal have been investigating water hardness removal using conductive concrete and metallic anode subjected to a range of power input. Previous project results from the PI’s lab showed 30% hardness removal at 15 V for 1 hr. trial. This project will expand the study to remove water hardness and soluble heavy metals like lead and chromium-6 without impairing the safety of drinking water. Also, the proposed technology will not require expensive water treatment facilities or extensive water pipe replacement. If combined with renewable solar power, it will be completely off the grid thus making the project eco-friendlier. Results: The project team will obtain the following information in optimizing the EP system using conductive concrete: 1) the optimum operating condition under batch and continuous flowing conditions, 2) system design parameters to treat extremely hard tap water, 3) heavy metal removal efficiency. Special care will be taken for data quantity and quality including redundant data collection and statistical analysis for data reliability.

grant.title: IntelligentSelf-Powered Wireless Sensing (ISPWS) System for Onboard Real-time Health Monitoring and Proactive Damage Detection of Freight Trains
grant.sponsor: The National Academies of Sciences Engineering Medicine
grant.abstract: Ensuring the safety of the freight railway network is essential for enabling the safe, reliable, and efficient movement of goods in the United States. Freight railcars are susceptible to wheel misalignment due to excessive speeding on curves, track defects, and failures of the critical components of their suspension systems that is usually caused by hunting oscillation, overheating, and impact. The current practice for condition monitoring of the critical components of freight railcars, such as wheel bearings, relies on trackside methods which are based on the deployment of sensors on the track in isolated locations. These methods are inherently “reactive,” implying that they resort to an unappealing find-and-fix strategy which act only when the target component is already damaged. In addition, they require a large amount of external power which makes them costly. The objective of this research proposal is to develop the proof-of-concept prototype of an onboard self-powered wireless sensing system for real-time health monitoring and prediction of the wheel bearings of freight railcars by employing a “proactive” damage detection strategy developed based on online machine learning . The wireless sensing system is battery-less and is powered by an onboard electromagnetic energy harvester with a high-power density.

grant.abstract: Traditional methods to stabilize expansive soil and aggregate bases use either lime, cement, fly ash, emulsion, or combination. However, with high levels of sulfates in soils in many areas in Texas, the traditional stabilizers have faced some problems. Many major pavement failures have occurred due to lime or cement induced sulfate in soils. Studies including TxDOT research showed there are potential benefits of applying polypropylene fiber to stabilize expansive clays and cement treated bases to increase strength, reduce chemical stabilizer content, and increase flexibility/ductility. However, the construction procedures and related specifications are not fully developed. To evaluate this promising technology, this research project shall perform eight objectives: 1) Verify test methods and application rates to be tested in the field through laboratory testing; 2) Select construction and test sites, with preference given to the Paris District for test sites; 3) Plan test section construction; 4) Develop construction specifications; 5) Monitor construction of test sections and verify that specifications are followed; 6) Monitor construction test sections quantifying, at a minimum, profile, FWD, and crack counts for two years post construction; 7) Prepare workshop training modules on construction and test methods; and 8) Present training workshops.

grant.abstract: The proposed ERC vision will be to develop a complete infrastructure for water conservation and management among energy industry, agriculture, and municipalities. There will be detailed water analysis on produced water and fracture fluid return from energy industry, water runoff from agriculture use, and greywater from municipality. The analysis will be summarized into a matrix that groups similar quality water products in order to generate a better perspective and overview of various water supplies. The next phase will be to employ various treatment strategies and determine the resulting water quality. These data will also be summarized in order to get a better perspective on achievements of each treatment technique. Based on literature review and detailed study on quality of water required for various applications (energy industry including petroleum (oil and gas), geothermal, agriculture, and municipality), a selection matrix will be developed on how the treated water can be utilized. A detailed study on the proximity of various industries will be conducted throughout the nation with emphasis on areas with greater density of oil and gas industry and agriculture. This analysis will indicate most optimal locations for synergy among the various stakeholders with greatest economical and societal impact. The impact of this water conservation/management on reduction of water disposal sites with possible contamination and seismic activities will be studied. In addition, the project will determine if there is a need to develop new technology or to combine existing treatment strategies in a new manner in order to achieve the required water quality given the influent water quality. Based on that determination, there might be work on developing those new methods to achieve the required objective. Furthermore, the quantity of water that can be conserved/managed among the various sectors nationwide will be determined, as that will measure the impact of this collaborative effort.

grant.abstract: Waste management is one of the most critical problems in various regions in the U.S. especially in the Lower Rio Grande Valley (LRGV) in the southernmost Texas on the border with Tamaulipas in Mexico. The U.S. produces 220 million tons of waste annually with an average of 2.1 kg per person each day (https://www.conserve-energy-future.com, 2019). The population in the LGRV is 1.2 million people with an estimated annual waste production of 2,500 tons annually. Traditional waste management refers to the activities used to manage waste from its inception until its final disposal. These activities include collection, transport, treatment and disposal of waste together with monitoring and regulation. However, most waste management strategies- if effective - remain unsustainable. Another contributor to the problem is that the current trend in manufacturing adopts the concept of throw-away consumerism in attempt to maximize the profit by producing one-time use products (https://www.conserve-energy-future.com, 2019). With many companies on the Texan/Mexican borders, there is a need for sustainable waste management strategies that focus on the reuse, recycling, and reducing the use of environmentally friendly materials. In LRGV, with the poor economic conditions, the aging infrastructure, and with approximately 15–20% of residents living in colonias, the problem of waste management exacerbates; and the concept of sustainable waste management strategies is nearly inexistent.

grant.title: Synthesis of Engineered Cementitious Composites (ECC) for Applications in Texas
grant.abstract: Among the groups of High-Performance Fiber-Reinforced Cementitious Composites (HPFRCC), Engineered Cementitious Composites (ECC) is a special type that is characterized by high-ductility (3-5% of strain) and moderate tensile strength (4-6 MPa) with 1.5-2% fiber contents by volume. Under tensile deformation, ECC shows a strain-hardening behavior and closely spaced microcracks after the first cracking. ECC has excellent shear capacity, improved damage tolerance, ability to control crack width, and synergistic interaction with reinforcing bars. The initial cost of ECC is higher than the regular concrete, but the use of ECC may reduce the life-cycle cost and corresponding environmental impact and provide improved safety because of the superior ductility. The objective of this project is to identify the applications in which the use of ECC can be applicable in Texas transportation system. To achieve this goal, the performing agency shall conduct seven tasks categorized into three activities: (1) a comprehensive literature review with in-depth meta-analyses, (2) a survey for state, federal, and international agencies, and (3) a cost-benefit analysis considering Texas environment, life-cycle cost, and environmental impact. Based on the collected data and analysis, the recommendations on ECC applications in Texas and considerations in mixture-design, production, and constructions of ECC shall be provided.

This proposed research will develop scalable and low cost graphenefiber hybrid composite membrane, therefore it will significant reduce the energy input for the RO process, by satisfying DWPR’s goal of “increasing water supplies by reducing the cost, energy consumption, and environmental impacts of treating impaired and otherwise unusable waters.” The requested fund will be used to support 0.25 month summer support (with 18% fringe benefits) for all three PIs, two graduate assistantships (with 10% fringe benefits), and three undergraduate scholarships. $5,600 will be requested to support faculty and students travel to Nano World Conference 2019 and ASME IMECE 2019, $12,000 will be requested to purchase raw materials and test supplies for membrane fabrication and water quality test, as well as ANSYS Mechanical license. $1,200 will be used to support Dr. Yuanbing Mao as an advisor to review our experimental data, quarterly reports and final report. The Lower Laguna Madre/Brownsville Ship Channel (LLM/BSC) Partnership was formed in 2014 and decided to develop a Watershed Protection Plan (WPP) to address the bacteria impairment and protect the primary contact use of the Lower Laguna Madre. An initial Watershed Characterization Report was completed under TCEQ contract 582-14-41167 from 2/12/2014 – 8/31/2018. Bi-monthly sampling of the Lower Laguna Madre, South Bay, and the Brownsville Ship Channel was also conducted for 2 years under TCEQ contract 582-14-41167. grant.abstract: Hurricane storm surge is an abnormal rise in sea level that destroys coastal lands due to the extensive eroding caused by the rapid flow circulation of a hurricane, as well as overland floods caused by the abnormal rise in the ocean. The storm surge is a definite threat to the Lower Laguna Madre (LLM), though it was fortunately spared by Hurricane Harvey. LLM plays a significant role as part of the United State Gulf Intracoastal Waterway by providing tourist attraction and natural habitats for marine life. A storm surge will not only damage the natural and man-made environment, but will impair the Texas economy as well. To fill the information gap regarding the impact of a hurricane storm surge on coastal inundation, we need more accurate and realistic prediction of storm surge flood event. We propose coupling the hurricane storm surge and watershed flood models by using the storm surge heights computed by the storm surge model as input data to the watershed flood model. The major outcomes of this proposed project consist of (1) improved coastal flood interactive GIS maps incorporating hurricane storm surge, (2) coupled hydrodynamic model to be used for the LLM hurricane storm surge and flow circulation prediction, and (3) improved local emergency evacuation routes based on coastal flood maps. grant.title: Sustainable Energy and Water Resource Management Program
Sustainable long-term performance of geothermal energy foundations in hot climates
grant.abstract: Overview: More widespread use of geothermal energy has the potential to reduce energy usage and the nation’s CO2 footprint. A geothermal energy foundation can be used to heat and cool a building by using heat exchangers installed within the foundation to extract energy from the earth to heat the building in the winter, and to transfer excess heat into the earth to cool the building in the summer. Energy foundations cost up to 20% less to install compared to traditional ground source heat pump (GSHP) systems. By using “free” energy, geothermal foundations reduce heating and cooling costs by 50–70% compared with conventional heating and cooling systems. However, when heating and cooling loads are imbalanced, such as in warmer climates or in high-rise structures where internal heat generation requires greater cooling capacity, the heat transferred into the ground surpasses the heat extracted, and the temperature in the soil around the geothermal foundation will gradually increase from accumulated heat. Scientific understanding is limited regarding 1) how accumulated heat changes soil properties by driving moisture away, reducing soil thermal conductivity, and causing lower heat transfer rates, subsequently reducing the energy foundation’s efficiency; and 2) how complex volume changes in the energy foundation and surrounding soil (due to moisture loss and thermal expansion) can alter soil-foundation interactions, affect geotechnical functions of the foundation, and cause displacements of the foundation and ground surface. To maintain the sustainable performance of geothermal foundations, it is first necessary to understand these responses, and later, to identify and evaluate solutions for dissipating heat in imbalanced heating/cooling conditions. The hypothesis of this research project is that changes in soil properties caused by accumulated heat will cause energy foundations to stop functioning after several decades, and a greater rate of imbalanced heating and cooling will correspond with shorter time-to-failure intervals. The objective of this project is to develop a verified thermal-hydro-mechanical 3D model that can be used to assess the effects of long-term accumulated heat on energy foundations and the surrounding soil. The proposed simulation experiments will be conducted using a fully coupled model developed in COMSOL® Multiphysics. Intellectual Merit: Findings from the proposed study will help the geothermal research community gain a better understanding of the effects of imbalanced heat on soil and geothermal energy foundations. Experimental data spanning 10 to 30 years are not available to study the long-term effects of accumulated heat in soil and energy foundations. Neither 3D modeling nor analytical solutions have addressed changes in soil properties caused by the foundation’s heat rejection, and therefore validated approaches are not available to address existing knowledge gaps. The planned activities will advance scientific knowledge by providing a more comprehensive understanding of the variables and conditions affecting energy foundation efficiency. These findings will also enable future investigations to explore changes in soil-foundation interactions (such as vertical and lateral load transfers), assess ground surface displacement, and evaluate solutions for reducing long-term heat accumulation in the surrounding ground. Broader Impacts: This proposal will yield two broad societal impacts. First, environmental and economic benefits will result from improved knowledge regarding the design, monitoring and maintenance of geothermal energy foundations. Effective design and use of these foundations reduces CO2 emissions, energy usage, and national reliance on non-renewable energy sources. Second, educational and outreach benefits from the integration of geothermal energy education in secondary and undergraduate settings will promote interest and engagement in STEM research. The project will engage students in grades 8-11 in the Texas Pre-Freshman Engineering Program (TexPREP) with instruction provided by research assistants working on the proposed project. Through the use of the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley’s Mobile Geothermal Educational Unit that was created for GSHP studies, the project also will increase public awareness of and engagement in STEM. All outreach activities will involve the PI’s interdisciplinary research team, which has thus far attracted two high school students and 28 civil, mechanical and electrical engineering undergraduate students (20% female and 94% Hispanic).

grant.title: System for Predicting South Padre Island shoreline Erosion
grant.abstract: We propose developing a numerical prediction system to estimate shoreline changes and dune erosion impacted by time scales of coastal storm events and arbitrary geometry alterations for coastal infrastructures. The system will compute coastal morphodynamic processes of ocean sediment transport, sand dune deformation, and cross sectional profile changes. The processes will be estimated based on hydrodynamic model computations of short/long wave transformation and dynamic currents, as well as hurricane storm surge and coastal inundation. We are proposing to build the morphodynamic computational model by using the XBeach model, which is a public domain numerical code developed by open source community with major funding from U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, UNESCO-IHE, and Deltares. With existing supports of the TGLO CMP #23 program, we will develop the hydrodynamic model of the South Padre Island vicinity area. To improve the modeling efficiency, we will couple the XBeach coastal morphodynamic model with the hydrodynamic model. The coupled model will maximize computational accuracy of shoreline changes and dune erosion during hurricane storm surge along the 32.2 miles of South Padre Island.

Experiential learning also includes field excursions to promote in-depth understanding of soil genesis, soil morphology, and land use. Additionally, our new and innovative Community Engaged Scholarship & Learning Experiences program enhances students’ professional competences as they solve local agricultural, soil quality and soil health challenges. grant.title: An engineered hydrologic cycle for fresh water from oceans
grant.abstract: Two-thirds of the world’s population face severe water scarcity (Sci. Adv. 2, e1500323, ’16). Existing desalination technologies (e.g., membrane-based, thermal-based, etc.) have various drawbacks on scale up, energy consumption, water quality, and environmental impact (Water Res., 75, 164, ’15). Emerging technologies for collection of airborne water are limited to small-scale production (Science, 356, 430, ’17). Mother Nature feeds the globe with freshwater by extracting it from oceans through the hydrologic cycle (HC) – evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. We propose an engineering research project to engineer the HC at an ocean site for utility-scale freshwater production. Simply put, moist warm air over the ocean surface continuously enters a downward flow passage and reaches a certain water depth, where the air is naturally cooled by chilled ocean water and the airborne water is collected through condensation. The cold dry air then runs through an upward flow passage, escapes at the warm ocean surface, and recovers temperature and humidity. The uniqueness is on realizing a fully nature-powered engineered HC: winds to feed the site with inexhaustible moisture-laden air, waves to drive the air through the flow passage, the temperature gradient of the ocean water to provide cooling for condensation, and the solar energy to power humidity replenishment.

grant.title: Energy Foundations' Heat Accumulation Impacts on Soil Properties, Structural Performance and Long Term System Efficiency
grant.abstract: Overview: A geothermal energy foundation harvests sustainable geothermal energy to heat and cool a building by using ground heat exchangers integrated into a building’s deep foundation that extracts energy from the earth to heat the building in the winter and injects excess heat into the earth to cool buildings in the summer. The energy foundation will save up to 20% of initial installation cost when compared with a traditional ground source heat pump (GSHP) system. By using this free energy, the energy foundation reduces heating and cooling costs by 50–70% compared with a conventional heating and cooling system. When the heat injected into the ground surpasses the heat extracted, or the cooling and heating load is imbalanced, the temperature in the soil around the energy foundation will gradually increase after each year of operation. There exists a lack of comprehensive understanding on i) how accumulated heat changes soil properties, drives moisture away, reduces soil thermal conductivity, and lowers the heat transfer rate resulting in a reduction of energy foundation efficiency, ii) how the complicated volume change in soil from moisture loss, thermal expanding and contracting, as well as how volume changes in the energy foundation can alter soil-foundation interaction and bearing capacity. Intellectual Merit: Neither experimental data, 3D modeling, nor analytical solutions are available for long-term and large-scale analysis of a complete energy foundation to address the addressed lack of comprehensive understanding. The hypothesis of this research is that due to the changes in soil properties and heat transfer rate caused from the accumulated heat, the energy foundation will stop functioning after several decades. The simulation experiment will be conducted using a coupled thermal-hydro-mechanical 3D model developed in COMSOL® Multiphysics. The validated model will be used to analyze the behaviors of soil and structures under a long-term imbalanced heat injection from an energy foundation with multiple energy piles, considering the effects of ground water movement. This helps achieve two research objectives 1) to understand the long-term behaviors of soil in terms of changes in temperature, moisture content, thermal conductivity and volume due to complex coupled thermal, hydraulic and mechanical interactions considering underground water movement and 2) to predict the long-term system performance of an energy foundation in terms of heat pump efficiency, foundation bearing capacity and stress, and settlement. The successful completion of this research will help the geothermal research community gain a comprehensive understanding of the effects of imbalanced heat on the soil and energy foundations. Broader Impacts: The broader impacts of this proposal include two major areas: 1) The broader use of energy foundations has the potential to reduce energy cost and the nation’s CO2 footprint. 2) This project will integrate geothermal energy education with the Texas Pre-Freshman Engineering Program (TexPREP) and University of Texas Rio Grande Valley’s (UTRGV)’s Hispanic Engineering, Science, and Technology Week (HESTEC). The proposed educational plan will increase public awareness and engagement with STEM through the use of an available Mobile Geothermal Educational Unit created for GSHP studies, the HESTEC exhibit, and TexPREP field trips for students in Grades 8-11. All activities will involve the PI’s interdisciplinary research team, which has attracted 25 civil, mechanical and electrical engineering students, among them 20% are women and 89% are bilingual.

grant.abstract: The project aims to explore a new process to get fresh water from oceans. The process is to be fully powered by the oceans themselves by means of the temperature gradient and waves. It does not use membranes to desalinate seawater. It does not produce brine either. Rather, it mimics the earth’s hydrologic cycle to a certain extent. Specifically, above an ocean surface warm air gains high humidity through natural solar heating. Below the ocean surface the water temperature naturally decreases with increasing water depth. By forcing the moisture-laden warm air to circulate through a cooling path down to the cold ocean at a certain depth, condensation occurs and fresh water is collected. The air circulation is driven by ocean waves. With the help of winds, inexhaustible moisture-laden air can continuously move into the dehumidification site, making large-scale fresh water production possible.

The goal of this research is to provide TxDOT with a proposed modified p-y models that can produce reliable designs of large-diameter drilled shafts for bridge foundations with different soil conditions. The main concern is that some repair attempts have shown a recurring failure of the repaired slope. To solve this problem, this research project has two set objectives: 1) evaluation of the existing repair methods and 2) recommendation of appropriate implementation procedures for several rapid repair methods for slope failure. This research proposes the evaluation of the various methods used for rapid repair of embankment failures using the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP). The work plan starts by surveying the existing rapid repair methods, defining their attributes, and their relative importance. A survey will be designed to solicit the experts’ opinion regarding TxDOT preferences to determine the relative weights through pairwise comparisons. For the decision criteria of the cost and time, the method of slices and finite element methods with the most suitable parameter inputs shall be used to obtain the typical failure modes of recently damaged slopes in Texas. This study will document the procedures of the different repair methods used for the slope failure modes to ensure the satisfactory long-term performance of the repair.

grant.abstract: We propose to design and develop a hybrid process comprising a completely mixed mesophilic anaerobic codigestion of food and yard waste, and a self-regenerating catalytic process to remove the toxic organic pollutant from the liquid digestate. The simplified process diagram is shown in Fig.1. Due to mechanical limitations, a completely mixed system can efficiently mix only those wastes with less than 10% solids contents. Usual solids contents of high organic substrates such as food waste are much greater than 20% and dilution should accompany the codigestion of these substrates in the completely mixed system. Final liquid digestate is usually used for diluting feed waste but high ammonia in the liquid digestate may overload the system leading to system upset. In this regard, dilution water needs to be low in organic and toxic chemicals. The proposed catalytic chemical reaction can effectively remove organic pollutants and chemicals from the liquid digestate using renewable energy. In addition, catalyst can be synthesized with nanoporous biocompatible and sustainable materials. The proposed technology involves synthesis of an ideal nanostructured self-activated catalyst with or without quantum dot (QD) arrangement, and biocompatible functionalization of the supporting materials. This functional material would lead to the greatest enhancement of the catalytic cleaning kinetics of the toxic digestate. By modifying the nanoporous photoactive catalyst and/or QD arrangement (pure CdS, pure CdSe, or a mixture of CdS-CdSe) with or without organic/inorganic ligand, the noble metal-based dopant, and the catalyst functionalization (–OH, –COOH, etc.), we will extract the information necessary to determine the faster photocatalytic cleaning and transport kinetics. We propose to develop an efficient hybrid codigestion process with understanding of the underlying mechanisms that govern these photocatalytic processes. Proposal Justification and Objective The objectives of the project are to optimize the anaerobic codigestion system by synthesizing an efficient Quantum Dot (QD) (CdS, CdSe, Cds-CdSe etc.) and combining it with photoactive nanostructured hybrid-materials to prepare efficient, self-regenerating stable materials that will produce clean water for reuse/dilution, solid waste for safe disposal or agricultural use and bio-gas for energy applications (Fig. 2). There are several advantages to incorporating QDs into photoactive semiconductor (such as TiO2, SiO2, etc.) materials. We propose a hybrid semiconductor supporting material for treatment and self-regeneration processes. First, QDs lower the bandgap of the composite semiconductor phase when compared to bare TiO2. QD-sensitized photoactive phase exhibits unique potential capability to produce quantum yields >1 by impact ionization (inverse Auger effect). Secondly, when a QD is combined with inorganic (or –organic) hybrid ligand, this leads to enhancement in short circuit current density and the ability to sustainably tune the stability of the electron-hole recombination process. The development of a biocompatible materials-based photoactive nanostructured support, which exhibits excellent optoelectronic properties toward stable electrocatalytic reactions, is especially suitable for enhanced photocatalytic decomposition performance in treatment of organic toxicants. We expect the following objectives from the proposed study: 1. Development of a new anaerobic codigestion system with liquid digestate recirculation for feed waste dilution. 2. The treatment of liquid digestate with a catalytic chemical reaction, which uses green and renewable energy to protect our water system. 3. Optimization of operational data of a completely mixed anaerobic codigestion system treating high organic food waste and yard waste. 4. Performance data of mesophilic anaerobic codigestion system under different operational conditions including different feed sizing, feed pretreatment methods, and feed mixing ratio. The proposed research can provide a new approach to codigestion for municipalities in which landfilling is the only economical choice for removing final digestate and there is a need for cost reduction in daily operation and maintenance.

grant.abstract: The four counties in deep south Texas known as the Rio Grande Valley are home to one of the fastest growing populations and one of the fastest growing manufacturing sectors in the state of Texas and world. The region is known as the Rio Grande Valley because it is located on the northern banks of the Rio Grande River which serves as the international boundary between the United States and Mexico. The Rio Grande Valley is also home to the second largest federally certified Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI) of higher education in the United States, the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). Approximately 90% of the more than 25,000 UTRGV students are Hispanic. The UTRGV College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) has been recognized for the quality of its academic programs and the numerous partnerships and collaborations that its faculty have established with more than 100 entities in its service area including manufacturers, local governments, economic development councils, two year institutions of higher education and not-for-profit organizations. The undergraduate degrees that the CECS awards in civil engineering, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, manufacturing / industrial engineering and computer science engineering are all accredited by the Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology (ABET). There is a tremendous need for the creation of the South Texas Industrial Assessment Center (South Texas IAC). In spite of the Rio Grande Valley’s rapidly growing population and the growing manufacturing sector the closest Industrial Assessment Center (IAC) to deep south Texas is 350 miles away. The development of the South Texas IAC will provide industrial energy assessments to small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs) that previously did not have access to such no-cost energy assessments. Through the provision of these industrial energy assessments the South Texas IAC has the potential of assisting manufacturers to save millions of dollars each year in energy and water management costs. The proposal to develop a South Texas Industrial Assessment Center (South Texas IAC) described herein is made possible because of a number of CECS engineering faculty who possess the requisite expertise and willingness to work with 20 UTRGV engineering students to carry out twenty industrial assessments per year. The faculty participating in the activities being proposed herein represent all of the departments in the CECS including electrical engineering, manufacturing and industrial engineering, civil engineering, and mechanical engineering. The diversity of faculty members’ areas of specialization and their various departmental affiliations in the CECS will provide students with an appreciation of the cross disciplinary nature of industrial energy assessments. The diversity of faculty will also ensure that engineering students throughout the CECS will become aware of the existence of the South Texas IAC and will have the opportunity to participate in the assessment activities as well as internships and research projects that come about as a result of the creation of the South Texas IAC. As manufacturing enterprises in the Rio Grande Valley become aware of the tremendous financial benefits that accrue to them from the energy assessments offered through the South Texas IAC it is anticipated that small and large manufacturers alike will contribute to the financial viability of the South Texas IAC after grant funds expire.

grant.abstract: One of by-products of anaerobic digestion (AD) system is renewable biogas. As biogas production through AD has been increasing in US and Europe, there is unbent need for optimization AD system in terms of process stability, higher methane yields, and inhibition problems including high ammonia in feed waste. Biogas is usually consisted of 50 to 65% methane and it can be converted into energy and heat via combined heat and power (CHP) system. Due to technical limitation, CHP system can only accept cleaner biogas containing much less moisture, hydrogen sulfide and siloxane than untreated biogas and it necessitates expensive gas treatment equipment. Biochar is a stabilized charcoal created by heating biomass under limited or no oxygen condition (pyrolysis). By the charring the biomass, much of the carbon becomes “fixed” into a more stable form that can minimize carbon dioxide emission to the atmosphere. In recent years, the potential use of biochars for soil amendment (Liang et al., 2008), long-term carbon storage (Lehmann, 2007), and contaminant removal (Mohan et al., 2014) has been receiving many attentions from scientists and funding agencies (e.g., USDA and NSF). Recently one of US national laboratories developed a novel biogas upgrade technology using biochar derived from organic wastes such as corn stover and woody material (Shen et al., 2015 and 2016). According to their research, AD system receiving biochars as additive produced biogas containing up to 90% methane and less than 5 ppm hydrogen sulfide, which can maximize the efficiency of the AD system. Porous structure and large surface area of biochar was found to sequester carbon dioxide and other impurities in biogas, thus improving biogas quality without additional downstream gas treatment. It was also claimed that biochar helped stabilize the digester performance by reducing ammonia toxicity and providing important minerals for microbes. We propose a research to test the synergetic effect of biochar to AD system using biochar derived from citrus peel and palm tree waste, which are commonly available in the valley area. The proposed study will benefit wastewater treatment and renewable biogas energy facilities by achieving following: 1. Finding process limitations of proposed anaerobic digestion enhancement using biochar. 2. Providing data specific to the use of locally available biomass wastes as to economically enhance conventional waste treatment system and upgrade renewable biogas to pipeline quality. 3. Developing an alternative biogas upgrade technology that eliminates needs of expensive downstream biogas treatment equipment. Proposed research will combine the expertise from two junior faculty members at CIVE and SEEMS. CIVE is one of the fast growing program in engineering and PI’s expertise on wastewater treatment will be combined with co-PI’s ongoing biochar research. With increasing regional/national emphasis on energy and environmental quality, this proposal will serve as a platform to accelerate the research productivity from both faculty members.

grant.abstract: An energy foundation harvests sustainable geothermal energy to heat and cool a building by integrating a ground heat exchanger into the building’s foundation. The goal of this Faculty Early Career Development (CAREER) Program proposal is to develop an integrated research and educational program centered on an innovative high efficiency moisture-controlled horizontal energy foundation system for use in residential and commercial buildings. The energy foundation will save up to 20% of initial installation cost when compared with a traditional horizontal ground source heat pump system, and by using free energy, reduce heating and cooling costs by 50–70% when compared with a conventional heating and cooling system. To this end, the objective of this study is to optimize the system to provide significant cost saving. Three levels of testing to be conducted in parallel include: full scale in-situ testing, model testing and specimen testing. The field and model testing is to understand system performance, and the specimen testing is to develop a new thermally enhanced nanofiber-cement grout. Three-dimensional computational modeling and probability analyses employing Monte-Carlo simulation will also be conducted to optimize system configuration and quantify the system’s reliability.

grant.abstract: Biogas production can support sustainable communities by reducing methane emissions, improving water quality, producing a local source of renewable heat, electricity and fuel, and strengthening the local economy by reducing energy costs and generating revenue. Biogas production by anaerobic digestion (AD) system has been proven to effectively stabilize high strength organic wastes if operated in a proper manner. In recent years, byproducts from the anaerobic treatment of organic waste (renewable biogas and fertilizer quality digestate) have been spotlighted due to their renewable, greenhouse gas reducing and eco-friendly characteristics. It is common to see animal manures or sewage sludge as a feedstock for the AD system. Combining them with fish waste could be a sustainable feedstock in Texas Coastal Communities. Fish wastes have high valued organic carbon for methane production but also have limitation due to their high protein content (15-20 % of wet weight), which can be converted to ammonia nitrogen during the AD process resulting in a system upset by ammonia toxicity when excessively generated. Biochar can enhance anaerobic digestion performance by achieving better biogas quality, greater ammonia toxicity suppression thus promoting better digester stability, and potentially enabling to treat higher organic wastes without increasing size of treatment tank. Biochar is a charcoal created by heating biomass under limited or no oxygen condition (pyrolysis) and it has been receiving attentions for soil amendment, long-term carbon storage, and contaminant removal. In this project, biochar produced from wasted sugarcane residue will be added to the AD system, so there will be less monetary investment requirement for real field application. Overall objective of this project is to test the synergetic effect of biochar to a completely mixed AD system receiving fish wastes generated from Texas coastal communities. Phase 1 of this project will be carried out in batch AD systems treating primary sludge from a local wastewater treatment plant. During the first phase, multiple anaerobic batch reactors with different amounts of sugarcane biochar will be incubated at room temperature for 3 weeks. Phase I will determine optimum operational condition based on biogas generation, organic removal and process stability. Phase 2 of this project will be performed in more controlled environment. Completely mixed anaerobic digestion system will be built and predetermined amount of biochar will be added to understand the changes in the system performance as per different operational environments determined from Phase I. Variations includes treatment temperature, organic loading rate, and substrate composition. Based on the findings, we propose to upgrade conventional digestion system to codigestion system as the phase 3 of the study. Codigestion anaerobic digestion is the anaerobic waste treatment system treating combination of two or more organic wastes such as fish waste. Conventional AD system is not equipped to perform codigestion because high organic food loading can deter the stability of system performance. Biochar is claimed to help stabilize the digestion system by suppressing ammonia toxicity, from which the anaerobic codigestion system may benefit.

presentation.event: Active and Passive Smart Structures and Integrated Systems XVI
presentation.abstract: This paper studies the use of an energy-regenerative tuned mass damper (ER-TMD) to (a) passively control the displacement of the superstructure of a two-degree-of-freedom base-isolated building model equipped with rubber bearings and (b) simultaneously generate electric energy that can be used to power conventional sensors installed on the building to monitor its response during an earthquake. The proposed passive ER-TMD is composed of two parts: mechanical and electrical. The mechanical part consists of a proof mass which is attached to the superstructure through a spring-damper system, and the electrical part consists of an array of permanent magnets, a rectangular air-core copper coil, and a harvesting circuit designed to maximize the electric power outputted from the system. The total damping coefficient of the proposed ER-TMD, that is obtained by summing up the damping effects of the mechanical and electrical parts, is variable and depends on the intensity of the input earthquake. A parametric analysis is carried out to find the optimum damping coefficient of the proposed ER-TMD in term of the peak ground acceleration (PGA) of the input earthquake. The numerical results show that the proposed ER-TMD can keep the displacement of the superstructure in a safe level while being able to generate an average electrical power about 0.5 W which is large enough to power a conventional accelerometer when the building is subjected to earthquakes with intensities at a level as that of the Maximum Considered Earthquake (MCE) defined by ASCE 7–10.

presentation.title: Development of an Electromagnetic Energy Harvester to Power Wireless Sensors used in Transportation Infrastructures
presentation.event: ASCE RGV Branch
presentation.abstract: Traffic-induced vibration of transportation infrastructures is a reliable source of kinetic energy, which can be harvested to power conventional monitoring sensors and peripherals installed on these structural systems, thereby reducing some dependence on non-renewable energy. The highway statistics shows that the average daily vehicle miles travelled (VMT) in the US is more than 5 billion. This indicates that a massive source of kinetic energy lies unused in the national transportation network. This study focuses on the modeling, designing and testing of the prototype of a high-power density electromagnetic energy harvester (EMEH) to convert such a kinetic energy into electrical energy. The proposed EMEH utilizes the concept of using planar arrays of small permanent magnets (PMs) to achieve strong and focused magnetic field in a particular orientation. The arrangement of PMs is optimized through finite element simulations in this study. The EMEH consists of a rectangular thick air-core copper coil (AC) moving relative to two identical planar arrays of PMs located on its left and right sides. They are mounted inside two housings made of Aluminum. The PMs arrays are attached to an Aluminum base plate that is firmly fastened to the bridge vibrating in the vertical motion due to the passing traffic. The AC is also attached to the Aluminum base plate through a system of elastic springs. The harvested electric power is generated by the electromagnetic induction occurring in the AC when it moves relative to the left and right PMs arrays. This relative motion causes a change in the magnetic flux of the PMs passing through the AC and induces an electromotive force in the circuit as per the Faraday’s law of induction. This results in an electric current flowing in the copper wire of the AC whose direction varies with the motion of the AC. The harvested electric power can be increased by amplifying the amplitude of the vibration of the AC which can be done by matching the natural frequency of the AC to that of the bridge’s vibration. The performance of the EMEH is evaluated by testing of a proof-of-concept prototype in laboratory and field.

presentation.event: Transportation Research Board (TRB) 99th Annual Meeting
presentation.organization: The National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine
presentation.abstract: Conventional vehicles (CVs) fueled by petroleum — i.e., gasoline and diesel — notably contribute to greenhouse gas emissions imposing harmful external impacts, which can be potentially mitigated by the advent of electric drive vehicles (EDVs), especially plug- in electric vehicles (PEVs). Recent improvements in battery technology and increased availability of charging infrastructure can lead to higher rates of EDV adoption and consequently higher levels of household vehicle ownership. To have a realistic understanding of the role of EDVs on vehicle ownership, this paper attempts to investigate EDV adoption behavior as a vehicle added to or traded for an existing household’s vehicle(s). To answer this question, we suggest a two-level nested logit (NL) model, which yields vehicle transaction decision — no-transaction, add, sell, and trade — and fuel type of added or replaced vehicle — CVs, hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), plug-in HEVs (PHEVs), and battery electric vehicles (BEVs). An empirical analysis using a dataset from California shows that the attentive persons to energy efficiency, represented by (potential) solar panels holders, are interested in added BEVs, replacement BEVs, replacement PHEVs, and added PHEVs followed by HEVs. Moreover, individuals’ perception of uncertain fuel price impedes them to add or trade in a BEV with more effects on added ones, while the major concern of added and traded-for PHEV adopters is perceived as less knowledge about this technology.

presentation.abstract: The prediction of inundations due to hurricane storm surge can be of great help for first responders andthe general public. The accurate forecast of inundations will require a system capable of working 24/7,have high standards of reliability and be stable. In case of a storm event the forecasting system willprovide a reliable and accurate data source for flooding maps. A flood forecasting system requires thelatest forecasting data regarding wind speed, direction and surface level pressure. The forecasting datathat will be used in this project is obtained from NOAA, more specifically, from the North AmericanMesoscale Forecasting System (NAM); a model that produces gridded forecasting data over NorthAmerica. The retrieved data from NAM needs to be processed before it can be used. The gridded dataneeds to be trimmed, interpolated onto a regular grid and processed to fit the input parameters for themodels involved. The models used for inundation prediction need to be coupled and automated to fitthe requirements of the project. The models that will be used are ADCIRC and HEC-RAS. These models,when coupled, will output the necessary data to create flooding maps. This data needs to be handledand superimposed onto an interactive base GIS map, which will be available for the public to access.The system will be constructed using popular tools for data processing and automation built on Python. In this way,the public will possess reliable forecasting flood maps and will be able to plan their actions ahead of unpredictable catastrophic disasters.

presentation.abstract: It is generally believed that safer roads will be a major benefit of autonomous vehicles (AVs). Recent AV-involved accidents in road tests and empirical evidence, however, suggest that travelers might still be concerned about the safety of a ride in an AV. It is further unknown whether and to what extent the travelers’ safety concern will hinder or promote the adoption of AVs. This paper makes a rigorous attempt to ascertain the causality between the travelers’ safety concern about the AV technology and their AV adoption behavior, in addition to exploring the determinants thereof. To this end, a recursive bivariate ordered probit model is estimated, which explicitly accounts for the endogeneity of safety concern in the AV adoption behavior. Drawing from a stated preference survey in the state of California, we find a significant negative association between safety concern and AV adoption. Important insights are also obtained into the impact on shaping travelers’ behavior of several socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, current travel behavior factors, and vehicle decision factors and attributes.

presentation.title: Autonomous Ridesharing and Parking: A New Multimodal Network Equilibrium Approach
presentation.event: Transportation Research Board 98th Annual Meeting
presentation.abstract: This paper models autonomous ridesharing and self-parking with autonomous vehicle (AVs). The model is structured as a leader-follower game, wherein a transportation network company (TNC) decides on fare, fleet size/allocation/relocation while anticipating travelers’ reactions in terms of market shares. Travelers’ decisions are formulated as a multimodal autonomous ridesharing and parking user equilibrium (MARPUE) comprising four components. A novel autonomous ridesharing user equilibrium (ARUE), which assigns travelers to shared AVs (SAVs) by accounting for ridesharing capacity using the section-based network representation, and by capturing one-to-many matching involved in ridesharing using the notion of search intensity. A new autonomous parking user equilibrium (APUE) that captures self-parking of private AVs. A modified user equilibrium (UE) for routing occupied AVs and human-driven vehicles (HVs), which accommodates road capacity improvement with (S) AVs. These components are bridged by a market share function. Numerical experiments reveal that the TNC, travelers, and system performance better off with ridesharing in terms of profit, total travel cost, parking demand, and network capacity.

presentation.event: Transportation Research Board 98th Annual Meeting
presentation.abstract: Maintaining good pavement conditions at airports are critical to ensuring safe operations of aircraft. In this study, gradient boosting machine (GBM), a fairly new machine learning technique, is employed to model and predict airport pavement conditions over time using data from Chicago O’Hare International Airport. Two GBM models are developed: one for runway pavements and the other for taxiway pavements. The models include various input variables encompassing pavement material, maintenance and rehabilitation history, weather conditions, and air traffic loading effects that influence deterioration of pavements. Development of the GBM models follows a systematic procedure consisting of model training, validation, and testing. The developed models yield high-accuracy PCI prediction for O’Hare. Given the promising results, similar models can be developed and implemented at other airports to cross validate field inspection results and reduce inspection time and cost.

presentation.abstract: Globally more than two billion people lack clean water. Currently 40% of the world’s population lives near the coast, where the hydrological cycle or water cycle, namely evaporation, condensation and precipitation, repeats. In the global hydrologic cycle evaporation from the water surface precipitates to produce rain and water vapor over the surface of the earth or plainly humidity, which is around 37.5 million billion gallons of water in total. The accelerated economic and pollution growth in the RGV is increasing the demand for drinking water. The RGV shares the major water resource, Rio Grande river, with Mexico. As RGV is more urbanized, quantity and demand of drinking water will be an issue along with water quality deterioration. This project will be, water harvesting from sea water by extracting the evaporated water from the ocean air. It is the exploitation of one of the first stages for hydrologic cycle, evaporated water from the ocean that become localized humidity in the air. Initial analysis thus far, most of condensed oceanic air was slightly acidic, which indicates that sea water vapor has dissolved carbon dioxide that causes water to be acidic. The RGV is growing rapidly and the alternative water resource needs to be addressed quickly before it suffers from the shortage of potable water. Efficiency and water quality from dehumidification will be analyzed for this project to determine viability of the dehumidification as a dire resource of water for the RGV.

presentation.title: Dynamic household vehicle decisions modeling with consideration of electric vehicles
presentation.event: Transportation Research Board (TRB) 97th Annual Meeting
presentation.organization: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
presentation.abstract: Plug-in electric vehicles (PEVs) offer alternatives to traditional vehicles that rely on petroleum-based fuels. While PEV customers can enjoy significant reductions in fuel costs, they incur a larger capital cost than users of traditional vehicles because PEV technology is still maturing. Therefore, consumers adopting PEVs face a trade-off between fuel cost savings with environmental benefits and extra capital cost. It is thus crucial for policy makers and PEV manufacturers to understand people’s vehicle decision-making process while considering their socio-economic and travel pattern characteristics as well as the built-environment factors. This paper presents a connected, two-stage, dynamic model of PEV adoption and vehicle-transaction decision-making. Two connected nested logit (NL) models are estimated. The upper level is a two-level NL model to predict choice of vehicle type between four fuel types: gasoline, diesel, hybrid gasoline–electric, and PEV. The lower level is an NL model of vehicle-transaction choice which accommodates four transaction decisions of buy, trade, dispose, and do nothing, while accounting for the log-sum from the vehicle-type choice model, and is estimated using two waves of a panel data set. We find that households with higher levels of income and education are more likely to adopt a PEV. We also found that primarily decision makers take into account the accessibility to charging stations as a critical factor in choosing PEVs.

presentation.title: Interaction between energy/water consumption and travel decisions in an activity-based framework
presentation.event: 15th International Conference on Travel Behavior Research (IATBR)
presentation.organization: Transportation Research Board: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
presentation.abstract: Given the ever-increasing levels of energy and water consumption worldwide and the consequent economic and environmental impacts, it is of critical importance to understand the factors affecting energy and water consumption. Despite the numerous studies in different fields on modeling energy and water consumption, there is a dearth of research in considering interactions between mobile (i.e., transportation) and stationary (i.e., residential) sources of energy and water consumption. In addition, the impact of individuals’ travel behaviors and activities on energy and water consumption have yet to be investigated. This paper integrates an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) model of residential energy and water consumption with the Agent-based Dynamic Activity Planning and Travel Scheduling (ADAPTS) framework based on in-home activities of agents. While traditional activity-based models mainly focus on out-of-home activities, the updated ADAPTS framework is capable of joint simulation of in-home and out-of-home activities of agents. In fact, agents could update their out-of-home activities according to their in-home activities and vice versa. Given the interaction of in-home and out-of-home activities, this paper is one step forward to link travel decisions, derived from out-of-home activities, and residential energy and water consumption based on in-home activities. An empirical analysis is conducted that relates the energy and water consumption of agents to their in-home activity type and duration, which highlights the roles of socio-economic characteristics and residential factors.

presentation.title: Investigating the impacts of mobility-on-demand services and green lifestyle on vehicle transaction decisions: a behavioral choice model with latent variables
presentation.event: 15th International Conference on Travel Behavior Research (IATBR)
presentation.organization: Transportation Research Board: The National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine
presentation.abstract: The significant share of private car use in the Americans’ trips (87% of daily trips and 91% of commute trips, according to the United States Department of Transportation (1)) highlights the key role of vehicle ownership decisions in shaping travel behavior. To better understand individuals’ vehicle decisions, one should also investigate the impacts of the ever-growing smartphone-based mobility-on-demand services and the non-vehicle transportation alternatives (i.e., bike, walk, and transit), in addition to the individuals’ characteristics and the vehicles’ features. This study addresses this need by focusing on the vehicle transaction decisions (i.e., longitudinal effects of historic vehicle decisions), among other dimensions involved in vehicle decision-making process (e.g., ownership, fleet size, body type, and vehicle usage). We contribute to the relevant literature by integrating a discrete choice-based model of vehicle transaction decisions with a latent variable model of individuals’ preferences for mobility-on-demand services and their “green lifestyle”. The latter factor reflects individuals’ attitudes towards non-vehicle transportation alternatives.

presentation.title: Shared mobility versus private car ownership: A multivariate analysis of public interest in autonomous vehicles
presentation.event: Transportation Research Board (TRB) 97th Annual Meeting
presentation.organization: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
presentation.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) are expected to hit the roads in the near-to mid-term future. Besides, shared mobility services such as car and ride sharing have been gaining momentum in recent years and show prospect for diminishing the need for private car use. Coupling these two emerging mobility trends, shared AVs could further remove the obstacles for widespread use of shared mobility services by providing a low-cost, convenient, and door-to-door travel mode comparable to private car. Therefore, it may be argued that future urban mobility is a public utility and AV private ownership may no longer be necessary. This paper aims to address this question and shed light on whether different mobility options of AVs have complementary, substitute, or no relationship. A multivariate ordered probit model, which accommodates the correlation between AV mobility options, is estimated using a stated preference data from the Puget Sound region in the Washington State. Specifically, the authors investigate public interest in considering AV as an owned asset as well as three shared mobility services: AV rental, AV taxi without a backup driver, and AV taxi with a backup driver present. We find that public interest in the four mobility options have complementary relationship and, thus, it is not true (at least at present) to assume that future urban mobility is purely a public utility. This study also examines explanatory factors including socio-economic, residential location, travel pattern, technology awareness, and psychological factors that shape public interest in AV mobility alternatives.

presentation.title: Corn stover, Orange peel, and pistachio shell biochars as a filter media for removing lead and arsenic in water
presentation.event: Annual meeting of the ASA-CSSA-SSSA-CSSS
presentation.abstract: The main threats to human health from heavy metals are associated with exposure to lead, cadmium, mercury and arsenic. This study evaluated three different biochars pyrolyzed with locally-sourced feedstock materials in South Texas as a filter media for removing lead (Pb) and arsenic (As) in water. Biochar is a highly porous charcoal produced by the combustion of biomass with limited or no oxygen (pyrolysis). Although biochar has been used as a soil amendment for a long time, the idea of using other feedstocks (e.g. plant biomass, manure, biosolids) to make biochars for water treatment is relatively new. The objective of this study is to 1) produce biochar from locally sourced feedstocks, corn stover (CS), orange peel (OP), and pistachio shell (PS), and 2) evaluate the biochar’s physico-chemical properties (pH, surface area, electrical conductivity, elemental composition, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, and Scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy). Feedstock materials were pyrolyzed under nitrogen conditions at temperature (300, 450, or 600°C). Our results showed that higher pyrolysis temperature resulted in higher surface areas for PS and CS biochars, which likely enhanced the adsorbent potential for lead (Pb). The optimal pH was found to be 6 for all biochar types in the solution pH range between 2 and 6 with percent Pb removal being 96% for CS, 95% for OP, and 19% for PS biochar. Biochars without surface modification was not effective in removing arsenic in water. Magnetized biochar was produced to evaluate its adsorbent properties for the arsenic removal in aqueous solution. Isotherm and pH studies were done to show the effectiveness of magnetic biochar in removing As (III) and As (V).

presentation.event: Annual Conference of Society of Wetland Scientists
presentation.abstract: Coastal wetland shoreline erosion is a continuing threat to the Texas Gulf and bay shorelines. This is caused by the constant tidal shifting that usually results in a landward deficit loss of important natural habitats as well as creating a danger for infrastructures and properties. Nonstructural shoreline erosion protection has been reviews as a successful coastal wetland management strategy both for erosion control and for maintaining healthy wetland habitat ecology. Mangrove forest is one of the most effective nonstructural shoreline protections in the Lower Laguna Madre, since it is a native species and filters heavy metals and toxic materials from wetlands and marsh area. In this study, hydraulic impacts of mangrove forest on the flow circulations near shorelines of the wetland protection to evaluate efficiency as the shoreline projection. Arturo Galvan coastal park, Port of Isabel recently built the Living Shoreline protection by equipping wetlands and marsh with black mangrove forest. A two-dimensional hydrodynamic model has developed to compute velocity vectors over the shallow wetland and marsh. High roughness coefficients assigned to represent the mangrove forest, which disrupts currents on the shallow water. The model solves the depth averaged Navier-Stokes equations using finite element method. Le Provost tidal constituents were adopted to implement the tidal driving force. Time dependent wetland flow transitions due to the mangrove forest will be presented.

presentation.abstract: Biochar is a highly porous charcoal produced by the combustion of biomass with limited or no oxygen. Biochar is viewed as an approach to carbon sequestration as much of the carbon in it is fixed into a recalcitrant form while improving soil structure in the long-term. There is also an increasing interest to use biochars for environmental remediation. While most of previous studies have focused on applications for wastewater treatment, there are limited studies on stormwater treatment. Stormwater in urban areas passes the impervious ground surfaces and carries pathogen, suspended solids, nutrients, heavy metals, and organic chemicals. To improve the effluent quality and harvest stormwater for non-potable use, bioretention and other means of low impact development have attracted many interests. Biochar can be a promising filter media due to its high adsorption capacity. This project aims to evaluate plant-derived biochars as a filter media for stormwater treatment. Contaminants of interest are nutrients (phosphate and nitrate) and heavy metals (copper, lead, and zinc). Three different biochar materials (oak tree, wheat straw, and wood biochars) will be compared to a commercial activated carbon as filter materials. Preliminary results from batch adsorption experiments using the four filter materials and their characterization by X-ray micro computed topography will be presented in context of their potential for stormwater treatment.

presentation.abstract: Urban stormwater runoff is often contaminated by heavy metals and nutrients as it washes through different impervious surfaces. Contaminants in stormwater runoff can be treated by various conventional physicochemical techniques (e.g., chemical precipitation, ion exchange, eletrodialysis, and reverse osmosis). However, most of these methods are either economically unfavorable, technically complicated, or spatially too limited. In urban settings, it is often difficult to provide an area that is adequate to have detention storage pond. Therefore, the use of a filtration system has received greater attention to remove contaminants within a smaller space. The purpose of this study is to compare different types of relatively low-cost charcoal-derived adsorbents to remove stormwater contaminants: commercial activated carbon, oak tree biochar, wood biochar, and wheat straw biochar. Contaminates in interest were heavy metals (Zn, Cr, and Cu) and nutrients (NO3-N, PO4-P).
